title: Polynomials
prerequisites: Comfort with algebraic expressions and like terms.
Knowledge of the laws of exponents.
Ability to substitute a value into an expression.
Familiarity with factorisation of simple expressions.

topics.title: Polynomials, Degree and Zeroes
topics.quick_summary: A polynomial is an algebraic expression in which the powers of the variable are whole numbers, and a zero of a polynomial is a value of the variable that makes it equal to zero.
topics.real_life: The path of a thrown ball is described by a quadratic polynomial, and its zeroes are exactly the two moments it is at ground level.

detailed.definition: A polynomial in one variable x is an expression of the form aₙxⁿ + ... + a₁x + a₀ where the coefficients are real numbers and n is a whole number. The degree is the highest power of the variable appearing with a non-zero coefficient.
detailed.key_idea: The powers must be whole numbers. Expressions such as x^(1/2) or 1/x are not polynomials, however algebraic they look — this is the single most common classification error.
detailed.working_principle: A number k is a zero of p(x) if p(k) = 0. A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes, and a linear polynomial has exactly one.
applications: The zero polynomial has no degree defined; a non-zero constant has degree 0.
Zeroes of a polynomial are the x-coordinates where its graph meets the x-axis.

points: Powers of the variable must be whole numbers for an expression to be a polynomial.
Degree = highest power with a non-zero coefficient.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.
A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, x = −b/a.
The degree of the zero polynomial is not defined.
mistakes: Calling √x + 3 or 1/x + 2 a polynomial; fractional and negative powers are not allowed.
Saying the degree of a non-zero constant is undefined; it is 0.
Confusing the value of a polynomial p(k) with a zero of the polynomial.
topics.memory_hook: 'Whole-number powers only' — that one rule decides whether an expression is a polynomial.
topics.advanced: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees that a degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots when complex numbers are allowed. The 'at most n' rule of school algebra becomes 'exactly n' once the number system is complete.

topics.title: Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem
topics.quick_summary: The remainder theorem gives the remainder on dividing p(x) by (x − a) as p(a), and the factor theorem says (x − a) is a factor exactly when p(a) = 0.
topics.real_life: Checking whether a large polynomial has a particular factor takes one substitution instead of a full long division — the theorem turns pages of work into a single line.

detailed.definition: Remainder theorem: if a polynomial p(x) is divided by the linear polynomial (x − a), the remainder is p(a). Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0.
detailed.key_idea: The factor theorem is simply the remainder theorem with remainder zero. Recognising this means only one idea has to be remembered, not two.
detailed.working_principle: To factorise a cubic, guess a small integer zero from the factors of the constant term, confirm with the factor theorem, divide out the linear factor, and factorise the remaining quadratic.
applications: To divide by (ax + b), evaluate p(−b/a), not p(b/a).
Factorising x³ − 3x² − x + 3 begins by testing x = 1, which gives zero.
Splitting the middle term factorises a quadratic without any division.

points: Remainder on division by (x − a) is p(a).
(x − a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0.
For divisor (ax + b), the relevant value is x = −b/a.
Try factors of the constant term first when hunting for a zero.
Splitting the middle term: find two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b.
mistakes: Substituting x = a when dividing by (x + a) — the correct value is x = −a.
Using p(b/a) instead of p(−b/a) for the divisor (ax + b).
Forgetting to factorise the quotient completely after removing one factor.
topics.memory_hook: 'Set the divisor to zero, substitute, and read the remainder.'
topics.advanced: Synthetic division carries out the same computation with only the coefficients, and is far faster for repeated testing. It is the algorithm behind most computer routines for polynomial root-finding.

formulas.name: Remainder Theorem
formulas.variables: p(x) = the polynomial, a = the value that makes the divisor zero.
formulas.when_to_use: To find a remainder without performing long division.
formulas.common_mistakes: Getting the sign of a wrong for a divisor of the form (x + a).
formulas.shortcut: Set the divisor equal to zero and solve for x — that is the value to substitute.

formulas.name: Algebraic Identities
formulas.variables: a and b = any algebraic terms.
formulas.when_to_use: For rapid expansion and factorisation without long multiplication.
formulas.common_mistakes: Writing (a+b)² = a² + b² and omitting the middle term.
formulas.shortcut: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca); if a+b+c = 0 then a³+b³+c³ = 3abc.
